extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of journalism history; scholars of early American print culture
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive standards and practical features of American colonial newspapers (1690–1765), covering format, production, content selection, editorial practice, and distribution. Useful for evaluating or reconstructing how early newspapers were produced and what readers expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement of foreign reports and literary extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in the selection and arrangement of foreign reports and literary extracts from English magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tire Journal 'showed unusual skill in the selection and arrangement of its foreign reports and literary extracts.' Editors compiled and arranged overseas material to form coherent accounts—this was judged a mark of editorial ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between news content and advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a paper devotes pages to advertising versus news: prosperous papers often filled most pages with advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: By 1760 the New York Mercury was 'often filling five of its six large pages with advertising.' Heavy advertising patronage could lead to occasional six- or eight-page issues; editors had to manage space tradeoffs between ads and editorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page format and sheet size
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of folio or crown sheets (four pages ~16x10 or 17x10 inches) versus smaller sheets or half-sheets in smaller towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 1765 most papers in larger towns used folio/crown sheets; smaller towns often used pot or foolscap sheets. Occasional issues expanded to six or eight pages to accommodate advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print quality (type, ink, presswork)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition of type, quality of ink, and presswork which affect legibility and aesthetics; smaller papers often used worn type and inferior presswork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The smaller American papers often used worn type, and ink and presswork were sometimes inferior. Caslon faces improved appearance about 1750; mixing type sizes sometimes occurred because of limited supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page ornamentation and cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of emblematic cuts, factotums (ornamental initials), and other decorative devices on the front page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front pages were frequently 'dressed up' with emblematic cuts set at ends or in the middle of the title (royal arms, ships, postriders). Factotums (initials enclosed in ornamental borders) and large initials were typographic conventions for important articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline practice versus simple date lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Headings were usually little more than date lines; anything like modern headlines was rare and typically short and single-column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label heads of two to four lines of fairly large type were unusual. The norm was modest headings; extravagant headline display was exceptional (example: Maryland Gazette's dramatic birth announcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography consistency and type-size constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency of type sizes and choice of typefaces constrained by available supplies; printers sometimes set papers in two or three sizes of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally a printer was forced to use mixed sizes 'not in order to display one article more than another, but because he had too small a supply of any one size.' Adoption of Caslon improved appearance around 1750.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper supply constraints affecting layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of paper influenced layout decisions, sometimes forcing odd devices like printing news/ads on margins with vertical lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of adequate paper supply led to the bad device of printing on margins with lines running vertically. Most printing-paper was imported from England; colonial papermills were small and crude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on imported materials and limited domestic manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on imported paper, ink, presses, and type, with only a few small colonial papermills and limited local manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper and printer's ink were mostly imported; presses and type mostly came from England. The first American papermill (Germantown, 1690) did not supply large colonial demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing technology and production capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Type of press (wooden screw press), inking method, number of presses, and realistic impressions/hour determine output capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presses were like Gutenberg's: wooden with lever-operated screw; two hundred impressions an hour was good work. Larger shops might have two or three presses; inking by sheepskin balls; pulling the lever required strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of printers as editors and entrepreneurial publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers ordinarily edited and published their papers and ran them as part of broader commercial enterprises (bookstores, job-printing, postmaster duties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With few exceptions, eighteenth-century American newspapers were edited and published by printers. Editors functioned chiefly as entrepreneurs, often selling books, coffee, patent medicines, acting as postmasters, magistrates, or lottery agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing and apprenticeship system
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of apprenticeships (commonly seven years), early starting ages, wages, and the pathway from apprentice to journeyman to shop-owner affect the labor force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apprenticeship often began as early as twelve and lasted until twenty-one; at term completion one could become a journeyman or set up a one-press shop with ~£75–£100. Apprenticeship conditions were often harsh and led to advertisements offering rewards for runaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contributors, pen-names, and writer 'clubs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers frequently relied on outside contributors, often writing under pen-names and sometimes organized into informal clubs supplying essays and serials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers compiled foreign news and miscellany by 'scissors and paste-pot.' Contributors were often professional men; groups included the 'Courantcers' (Hell-Fire Club) and the 'Meddlers' Club.' Some 'clubs' may have been literary pretence derived from The Spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts of news: history versus timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Two competing concepts of news: presenting events as an orderly 'history' (chronicle) versus emphasizing timeliness and newness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because overseas news reached colonies slowly, editors often subordinated timeliness to a history-concept (e.g., Campbell's 'Thread of Occurrences' or Parker's 'The History of Europe, &c.'). This shaped selection and presentation of foreign reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency and its impact on timeliness; use of supplements and 'extras'
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly schedules limited timeliness; editors sometimes issued supplements or broadsides (extras) to publish breaking news between regular issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly publication meant delays; examples: Franklin's July 7, 1755 'Supplement' about Fort Cumberland issued three days before the weekly. The first extra was the News-Letter broadsheet on the trial of pirate Quelch (1704).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary news sources and solicitation of letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on ship captains, letters from abroad, local correspondents (often postmasters), and exchanges with other newspapers as main information sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers solicited 'authentick' accounts and subscribed for London papers; correspondents in other towns supplied maritime and local intelligence. Letters carried overseas news via captains and merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercolonial news sharing and unattributed reprinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Common practice of using other colonial newspapers' items without credit to fill pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As intercolonial networks developed, printer-editors 'helped themselves to one another's news stories without credit,' mirroring earlier appropriation of foreign papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection bias against local minutiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency to neglect everyday local news because towns were small and events were already widely witnessed; newspapers focused on larger events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local items were often meagre: 'There were too many spectators there to make it now a piece of public news.' Editors printed deaths, storms, governor movements, but often omitted events for political motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content mix and topical priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical content distribution: foreign wars and politics (dominant), intercolonial/political documents, maritime news, public proclamations, religion, society notices (marriage, death), crime, epidemics; sports rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The French and Indian War and contests between assemblies and royal governors were major recurring stories. Maritime news was always important; public documents often crowded out other items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practices: scarcity of formal editorials and use of letters/pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Few formal editorials appeared; discussion of public affairs occurred through letters, signed pen-names, extracts, and separate pamphlets for extended argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin printed few formal editorials; he preferred pamphlets for extended proposals (e.g., currency reform). Newspapers published 'convenient Hints and Touches' and frequently carried political essays from contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy toward publishing personal controversy and paid controversialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied editorial policies on whether to publish personal attacks or private altercations; some editors refused, others allowed paid submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors resolved 'never to publish anything wherein the character or interest of any particular Person is concerned,' but most did not adhere. A common doctrine held that liberty of the press required opening columns to controversialists, especially when paid. Franklin refused to make his paper a 'stagecoach' for everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising placement and editorial sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical placement of advertising (often at the end) and editorial practices for appending fresh items (e.g., 'Postscript') after ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising usually came last in the paper; Franklin often followed ads with a 'Postscript' containing items from a later post, thereby using layout to append more timely advices after the main news and advertising sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual satire and cartoons for argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of cartoons and visual devices to reinforce editorial argument or political messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' snake cartoon (divided snake labeled for colonies) accompanied commentary about colonial disunion; such images 'immediately caught the popular fancy' and were reproduced elsewhere.
